ai_summary: Great Britain's wind generation currently stands at 5.5 GW, with Scotland contributing an estimated 2.9 GW, representing 28.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This abundant renewable output drives Scottish carbon intensity down to a remarkable 3 gCO2/kWh, standing in sharp contrast to the GB-wide carbon intensity of 191 gCO2/kWh. However, significant transmission bottlenecks between Scotland and England restrict the export of this clean electricity to southern demand centres. As a result of these network constraints, 12.3 GWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring an immediate constraint cost of about £391,153. To replace this locked-in green power, thermal generation was ramped up, resulting in an estimated 2,341,997 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and releasing an additional 4,314 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Extrapolating this daily constraint spending indicates an estimated total yearly cost of £143 million for curtailment. Ultimately, this structural limitation shifts costs onto consumers, translating to an estimated increase of approximately £0.50/MWh on everybody's invoice in the UK.
